## Type
Map

## Description
The figure is a map illustrating the alpine areas within New South Wales, Victoria, and Tasmania in south-eastern Australia. The map shows the coastline and state boundaries, with dashed lines indicating the northern and western limits of the depicted region.

The landmasses are delineated, with specific regions shaded in grey to represent "Alpine" areas.
*   The New South Wales and Australian Capital Territory region, in the north-east, features a large contiguous alpine area, primarily along the Great Dividing Range. This area includes numbered points 1 through 18. Major regional labels include "Northern Tableland", "Central Tableland", and "Southern Tableland". The city of Sydney is marked on the eastern coast.
*   The Victorian region, to the south-west of NSW, contains several distinct alpine areas, some of which appear to extend from the NSW areas. These areas include numbered points 19 through 25. The city of Melbourne is marked on a bay in the south.
*   Tasmania, an island state located south of Victoria across Bass Strait, shows three separate shaded alpine regions. These regions include numbered points 26, 27, 28, and 29. The city of Hobart is marked on the south-east coast.

The map includes lines of latitude and longitude for geographical reference. A legend indicates that the grey shaded areas are "Alpine". Below the map, "Figure Notes" and "Explanatory Information" provide additional context regarding the definition of alpine areas.

## Figure
Figure 10.2.15a: Typical enclosed stepped down shower construction (membrane below tile bed)

## Type
Section drawing

## Description
The figure is a cross-section detail illustrating a typical enclosed stepped-down shower construction where the membrane is located below the tile bed. The diagram shows the interface between the stepped-down shower area and the adjacent higher floor level, including a wall on the shower side.

From the bottom up, on the shower side, there is a "Floor substrate". A "Shower membrane" (represented by a dashed line) is laid over the floor substrate. This membrane extends horizontally across the stepped-down shower area, turns up vertically along the wall and the waterstop, and also extends horizontally under the adjacent higher floor structure. Above the shower membrane in the shower area is the "Tile bed" (hatched), which is topped with "Floor tile" (multiple thin layers).

A vertical wall is shown on the right side of the shower area, with "WP" (waterproof) indicated on its inner surface. A "Shower screen and track" is positioned on the "Floor tile" at the edge of the stepped-down area, which is also where a "Waterstop" is located. The waterstop is a vertical element embedded within the floor layers, acting as a barrier. The shower membrane turns up against the shower side of the waterstop and continues horizontally under the adjacent higher "Mortar tile bed" (hatched) and its "Floor tile" layer.

The diagram shows a step-down from the finished floor level outside the shower to the finished floor level inside the shower. The vertical distance of this step-down is indicated by a dimension line.

## Labels and annotations
*   Shower side
*   WP
*   Shower screen and track
*   Floor tile (appears twice)
*   Mortar tile bed
*   Waterstop
*   Tile bed
*   Shower membrane
*   Floor substrate

## Dimensions and values
*   25 mm min. (vertical distance from the finished floor level outside the shower to the finished floor level inside the shower)

## Notes
None shown

## Figure
Figure 10.2.15b: Typical enclosed stepped down shower construction (membrane above tile bed)

## Type
Section drawing

## Description
This figure is a cross-sectional view illustrating the construction of a typical enclosed stepped-down shower recess, specifically detailing a configuration where the shower membrane is located above the tile bed. The diagram shows the junction of a wall with a floor, differentiating between the "Shower side" (left) and the adjacent non-shower area (right).

Starting from the bottom, the floor structure includes a "Floor substrate". On the shower side, a "Tile bed" rests directly on the "Floor substrate". Above the "Tile bed" is the "Shower membrane", which extends horizontally across the shower floor and turns up vertically along the wall. "Floor tile" is laid on top of the "Shower membrane" within the shower recess.

At the transition point between the shower and the non-shower area, a "Waterstop" is installed vertically. It rests on the "Shower membrane" and rises to a level higher than the finished floor of the shower. The "Shower screen and track" assembly is positioned on the non-shower side of the waterstop, appearing to be anchored into the wall and sitting on the floor finish.

On the non-shower side, the floor structure consists of a "Mortar tile bed" laid on the "Floor substrate", and "Floor tile" laid on top of the "Mortar tile bed". There is a distinct step-down from the finished floor level of the non-shower area to the finished floor level of the shower area. A vertical dimension arrow indicates the minimum height difference between these two finished floor levels.

The wall structure is depicted with "WP" (waterproofing) on its inner face, extending upwards from the shower membrane.

*   Figure 10.2.15b: Typical enclosed stepped down shower construction (membrane above tile bed)

*   Shower side

## Figure
Figure 10.2.15c: Typical unenclosed stepped down shower construction (membrane below tile bed)

## Type
Section drawing

## Description
This figure is a cross-section drawing illustrating the construction details of a typical unenclosed stepped-down shower, specifically showing the membrane positioned below the tile bed. The drawing focuses on the transition from the shower area to an adjacent floor, including a frameless shower screen.

At the bottom, a Floor substrate forms the base. Above this, a Tile bed is laid, and on top of the tile bed, Floor tiles are installed. A membrane, indicated by a dashed line pattern, is shown located below the mortar tile bed and extends upwards to the level of the top of the adjacent floor construction.

Within the shower area, the floor level is stepped down. A vertical section marked 'WP' (Waterproofing) rises from the floor substrate. At the junction where the shower area steps down, a Waterstop is incorporated, positioned vertically at the extremity of the unenclosed shower area, extending from the floor substrate level up to the top of the tile bed. The membrane runs continuously across the floor substrate, up the vertical face of the step, and behind the waterstop, then continues horizontally under the tile bed and floor tiles in the shower area.

A Frameless shower screen is shown installed on the stepped-up edge of the shower area, supported by a Structural sealant support which sits on top of the membrane and tile bed. The screen extends upwards.

On the "Shower side" (the lower floor level), a Waterproof sealant is applied in the corner where the floor tiles meet the vertical wall (WP). A vertical dimension indicates a minimum height requirement for this waterproof sealant relative to the top of the floor tile.

## Labels and annotations
* Figure 10.2.15c: Typical unenclosed stepped down shower construction (membrane below tile bed)

* WP
* Waterproof sealant
* Floor tile
* Tile bed
* Floor substrate
* Frameless shower screen
* Structural sealant support
* Membrane below mortar tile bed
* Waterstop - position waterstop at the extremity of the unenclosed shower area

## Dimensions and values
* 25 mm min. (vertical height of waterproof sealant above the top of the floor tile)

None shown

## Figure
Figure 10.2.15d: Typical unenclosed stepped down shower construction (membrane above tile bed)

## Type
Section drawing

## Description
This figure is a cross-section drawing illustrating the construction of a typical unenclosed stepped-down shower where the waterproof membrane is positioned above the tile bed.

On the left, the "Shower side" features a wall labelled "WP" (Waterproof) and a floor assembly. The floor assembly consists of a "Floor substrate" at the bottom, topped by a "Tile bed", and then "Floor tile". A "Waterproof sealant" is applied vertically at the junction of the floor tile and the wall.

To the right, outside the shower area, the floor level is higher, creating a step down into the shower. A "Frameless shower screen" stands on a "Structural sealant support" at the transition between the two floor levels.

An L-shaped "Membrane above mortar tile bed" is shown in black, extending from the shower side, underneath the "Floor tile" and "Tile bed" layers, up the face of the "WP" wall, and then horizontally across the top of the stepped-down section, and down the side of the structural sealant support.

A "Waterstop" is depicted as an L-shaped profile embedded within the tile bed layers, positioned vertically at the extremity of the unenclosed shower area, beneath the membrane.

Below the drawing, there is text outlining requirements for "Hob construction", detailing acceptable materials and installation guidelines. It lists four acceptable materials for hobs: masonry, concrete, autoclaved aerated concrete, or extruded polyurethane foam. It also states that gaps, joints, and intersections of the hob substrate must be flush before membrane application, and hobs must be secured to the floor and sealed against the wall before membrane application.

## Labels and annotations
*   Figure 10.2.15d: Typical unenclosed stepped down shower construction (membrane above tile bed)
*   Frameless shower screen
*   Structural sealant support
*   Membrane above mortar tile bed

*   Floor substrate
*   10.2.16 Hob construction
*   (1) _Hobs_ must be constructed of—
*   (a) masonry; or
*   (b) concrete; or
*   (c) autoclaved aerated concrete; or
*   (d) extruded polyurethane foam,
*   in accordance with Figure 10.2.16.
*   (2) All gaps, joints and intersections of the _hob_ substrate must be made flush before application of a _membrane_.
*   (3) _Hobs_ must be adequately secured to the floor and sealed against the wall prior to applying a _membrane_.

## Dimensions and values

## Figure
Figure 10.2.16: Typical hob construction — internal membrane

## Type
Section drawing

## Description
The figure depicts a cross-section of a typical hob construction in a shower area, illustrating the placement of an internal waterproofing membrane.

On the left is the "Shower side", and the right side represents the adjacent floor area. At the base, a "Substrate" forms the foundation. A rectangular hob structure is built upon this substrate. The core of this hob, shown with diagonal hatching, is noted with the restriction "Timber must NOT be used for hob".

An internal "Membrane", indicated by a bold dotted line, encloses this hob core. It starts on the "Substrate" beneath the hob, extends vertically up the inner (shower) face of the hob, folds over the top of the hob, and then extends vertically down the outer face of the hob, stopping just above the "Substrate" level on the outer side. The membrane also extends horizontally to the left, beneath the "Mortar bed" on the shower side.

On the "Shower side", a "Mortar bed" sits on top of the "Membrane" and "Substrate", with an arrow indicating flow from the mortar bed towards the base of the hob. Tiles are laid on top of the mortar bed. The hob structure itself is finished with "Tiles" that cover its top surface and the outer (non-shower) vertical face, extending down to meet the adjacent floor level, which is also tiled.

At the top of the hob, a "Sealant" is applied in a joint between the top tiles of the hob and an adjacent element, labelled "Top of tray side", which is partially depicted with dashed lines. The membrane continues behind this sealant connection.

A horizontal dimension is indicated at the base of the outer (non-shower) side of the hob, showing the minimum horizontal extent of the membrane or hob beyond the outer face of the tiles.

## Labels and annotations
*   Figure 10.2.16: Typical hob construction — internal membrane

*   Timber must NOT be used for hob

## Figure
Figure 10.2.17: Typical hobless construction

## Type
Section drawing

## Description
The figure illustrates a cross-section of a typical hobless shower construction, focusing on the interface between the shower area (indicated as "Shower side" to the left) and the adjacent floor.
From the bottom, the construction starts with a concrete slab foundation. A waterproofing membrane is laid over the slab, extending upwards along the vertical leg of an L-shaped "Waterstop".
The "Waterstop" is embedded into the slab, with its vertical leg positioned at the boundary of the shower area.
"Tiles" are installed on top of the membrane and slab within the shower area.
A "Shower screen track" rests on the tiled surface, directly above the vertical leg of the waterstop.
A "Flexible sealant" fills the joint between the shower screen track and the adjacent tile on the shower side.
A detailed circle highlights the exact configuration of the waterstop, membrane, tiles, and shower screen track at the transition point.
The shower area floor, including the shower screen track, is depicted as being lower than the adjacent floor level.

## Figure
Figure 10.2.18: Typical termination of membrane at extent of shower area

## Type
Section drawing

## Description
This figure is a cross-section drawing illustrating the typical termination of a waterproof membrane at the boundary between a shower area and a general bathroom area. The drawing shows a floor assembly composed of an underlying floor substrate or bedding, topped by a membrane, and then a finished floor surface (implied by the sloped lines).

From left to right:
The "Shower area" is on the left, identified by a dimension line indicating a minimum distance "1500 mm min. from shower outlet" extending from the left boundary towards the right. Within the shower area, the finished floor surface slopes downwards towards the left, indicating drainage towards a shower outlet (not explicitly shown). The membrane layer is continuous and underlies the sloped finished surface in this area.

The "Bathroom area" is on the right. The finished floor surface in this area appears to be at a higher elevation relative to the lowest point of the shower area floor and also slopes, indicated by an arrow pointing to the right.

The transition between the shower area and the bathroom area is defined by a vertical waterstop barrier. The membrane from the shower area extends up the face of this waterstop on the shower area side, then turns horizontally to pass over the top of the waterstop, and then turns down the other side of the waterstop on the bathroom area side, where it terminates. The membrane is shown adhering to the floor substrate/bedding beneath the finished floor in both areas and across the waterstop. A detail circled at the waterstop shows the membrane continuing beneath the finished surface on both sides, and forming an L-shape over the waterstop. The finished floor surface terminates against the waterstop on both sides.

## Labels and annotations
*   Shower area
*   Bathroom area
*   Membrane
*   Floor substrate or bedding
*   Waterstop
*   1500 mm min. from shower outlet

## Dimensions and values
*   1500 mm min. from shower outlet

## Notes
Fall is to be provided in accordance with 10.2.12.

## Figure
Figure 10.2.19b: Typical preformed shower base/floor junction on timber floors, including particleboard, plywood and other timber materials

## Type
Section drawing

## Description
The figure is a section drawing illustrating a typical junction between a preformed shower base and a timber floor, including particleboard, plywood, or other timber materials.

On the left side of the diagram, a "Shower screen" is shown positioned above and slightly to the right of the curved, raised edge of a "Preformed shower base". The "Preformed shower base" slopes downwards to the left, indicating the interior of the shower. Beneath the sloping part of the preformed shower base, a "Shower base support" is indicated, resting on a "Shower side" area, which is part of the general timber floor structure. The "Shower side" is depicted with a cross-hatch pattern.

On the right side, representing the main bathroom floor outside the shower, a layered assembly is shown from bottom to top: "Floor substrate", then a "Membrane" layer on top of the substrate, followed by a "Tile bed", and finally "Floor tile" as the topmost layer. The "Floor substrate" is also shown with a cross-hatch pattern.

At the junction point where the preformed shower base meets the main floor assembly:
1. A horizontal layer of "Waterproof sealant" is shown as a solid black rectangle, resting directly on the "Floor substrate" and extending from beneath the vertical edge of the "Preformed shower base" outwards to the right, under the "Membrane" and "Tile bed".
2. The "Membrane" layer from the main floor assembly extends over and seals onto this horizontal "Waterproof sealant" layer.
3. A vertical application of "Waterproof sealant" is shown at the interface between the vertical edge of the "Preformed shower base" and the adjacent "Tile bed" and "Membrane" layers. This sealant fills the gap between the "Preformed shower base" and the "Tile bed", extending from the top surface of the "Floor tile" down to the "Membrane" layer.

## Labels and annotations

## Figure
Figure 10.2.2: Extent of treatment for shower areas — concrete compressed fibre-cement and fibre-cement sheet floors

## Type
Combination of plan views and side (elevation) views.

## Description
The figure illustrates the required extent of waterproofing treatment for shower areas when concrete, compressed fibre-cement, and fibre-cement sheet floors are used. It is divided into two main parts: (a) Enclosed shower and (b) Unenclosed shower.

**(a) Enclosed shower:**
This section shows the waterproofing requirements for a shower area enclosed by walls and a shower screen.
(i) **Plan view:** Depicts a square area with walls on the top and left sides. A "Shower screen" runs along the bottom and right sides, forming the enclosure. An 'X' crosses the square, intersecting at the centre where a circle is located. An arrow points from the top-left corner to this central circle. The entire floor area within the shower screen is labelled "Waterproof floor" and "WP".
(ii) **Side view:** Shows a vertical "Waterproof wall" with a shower head symbol protruding from it. A vertical dimension indicates the height of this waterproof treatment from the floor up the wall. A leader line points from the top of the waterproof wall segment to a label. Another leader line points to the vertical edge of the wall, labelled "Edge of shower screen".

**(b) Unenclosed shower:**
This section shows the waterproofing requirements for a shower area that is not fully enclosed by a screen, typically against a single wall.
(i) **Plan view:** Depicts a straight wall segment at the top with two shower head symbols along it. A semi-circular line extends outwards from the wall, defining the "Minimum extent of waterproofing" on the floor. A dimension arrow measures the radius of this semi-circle from the wall. The floor area within the semi-circle is labelled "Waterproof floor" and "WP".
(ii) **Side view:** Shows a vertical "Waterproof wall" with a shower head symbol protruding from it. A vertical dimension indicates the height of the waterproof treatment from the floor up the wall. A horizontal dimension indicates the extent of waterproofing on the floor, measured outwards from the wall.

## Figure
Figure 10.2.20: Typical bath junctions

## Type
Section drawing, detail

## Description
The figure illustrates three common bath junction types, focusing on the waterproofing and structural accommodation of the bath rim at a wall or a shelf.

*   **Part (a) Bath/wall junction - recessed:** This detail shows a bath where its rim is recessed into the wall structure. From left to right, the main body of the bath curves upwards. At the top of the bath's edge, a waterproof sealant is applied at the interface with the wall. Above this sealant, a layer of water-resistant surface material of the wall is depicted. To the right of the bath rim, a rebate is formed within the wall structure to accommodate the bath rim, allowing the bath to sit flush or partly within the wall plane.

*   **Part (b) Bath/wall junction - battened:** This detail shows a bath where its rim is accommodated by a batten fixed to the wall structure. Similar to (a), the bath's body curves upwards. A waterproof sealant is applied at the junction between the top edge of the bath and the wall's surface. Above the sealant, a water-resistant surface material of the wall is shown, backed by wall sheeting. To the right of the bath rim, a batten is fixed to the wall structure, providing support and accommodation for the bath rim.

*   **Part (c) Bath/shelf junction:** This detail shows a bath connecting to a tiled shelf. The bath's rim forms the left edge of the shelf. An enlarged circular detail shows the internal construction of the shelf from top to bottom. The top layer is a floor tile. Below the floor tile is a membrane. Below the membrane is a mortar tile bed, which rests on a shelf substrate. A waterproof sealant is applied at the junction between the bath rim and the floor tile. A water stop is positioned underneath the bath lip within the shelf structure, and it projects upwards.

## Figure
Figure 10.2.24: Typical bathroom door details for whole bathroom waterproofing

## Type
Isometric detail drawing

## Description
The figure presents two isometric detail drawings, (a) and (b), illustrating typical waterproofing details for a bathroom door at different stages of construction. Both drawings show a section through a door jamb, wall, and floor, highlighting the placement of the waterproof membrane and a waterstop. The perspective is looking towards the door opening from inside the bathroom.

**Part (a) - After installation of architrave:**
This drawing shows a vertical door jamb with an architrave installed over the adjacent wall surface. A waterproof membrane is applied vertically on the wall, underneath the architrave, extending down to the finished floor surface. The floor structure is depicted below the finished floor. At the threshold, an L-shaped waterstop is positioned on the floor, immediately outside the door jamb line. The waterstop's horizontal base is sealed to the floor, and its vertical upstand is flush with the finished floor surface. The waterproof membrane extends down to overlap and seal to the waterstop. An arrow indicates the waterstop's position relative to the overall waterproofing system.

**Part (b) - Prior to installation of architrave:**
This drawing is similar to (a) but depicts the stage before the architrave is installed. The vertical door jamb is visible, and the waterproof membrane is applied vertically on the wall surface, exposed where the architrave will eventually be. This membrane extends down to the finished floor surface. Similar to (a), the L-shaped waterstop is positioned at the threshold, with its base sealed to the floor and its upstand flush with the finished floor surface, receiving the waterproof membrane from the wall above. An arrow indicates the waterstop's position.

## Figure
Figure 10.2.27 (explanatory): Typical bond breaker details

## Type
Section drawing

## Description
The figure depicts two typical bond breaker details for internal corners where a membrane transitions from a vertical wall surface to a horizontal floor surface. Both details show a wall substrate or lining above a floor substrate or bedding.

The **upper detail** shows a bond breaker formed by a backing rod and continuous tape. A backing rod is positioned in the internal corner formed by the wall substrate or lining and the floor substrate or bedding. A continuous tape is applied over this backing rod to hold it in place and prevent the membrane from flowing around the rod. The membrane is then applied over the tape and backing rod, curving smoothly from the wall substrate to the floor substrate.

The **lower detail** shows a bond breaker formed by a dedicated bond breaker material. A bond breaker element (represented as a layered strip) is applied along the internal corner, extending from the floor substrate or bedding up the wall substrate or lining. The membrane is then applied over this bond breaker, curving smoothly from the wall substrate to the floor substrate.

## Figure
Figure 10.2.29: Typical membrane termination at drainage outlet

## Type
Section drawing

## Description
The figure depicts a cross-section of a typical membrane termination at a drainage outlet in a floor assembly. It illustrates how a membrane creates a waterproof seal around a drainage point.

From the top down, a membrane (shown as a dashed line pattern) lies over a floor substrate (shown as a solid layer). The membrane and floor substrate extend horizontally from the left and right edges towards the central drainage outlet. At the outlet, the floor substrate is recessed downwards, forming a stepped U-shaped cavity. A drainage flange, also with a stepped profile, is nested within this recessed floor substrate. The membrane follows the contours of the floor substrate and the drainage flange, extending down into the flange and folding over the top edge of the flange. The membrane covers the entire internal surface of the drainage flange down to its lowest point. Below the drainage flange, a drainage pipe connects vertically upwards into the bottom of the flange, indicating the flow path for water.

## Labels and annotations
*   Membrane
*   Floor substrate
*   Drainage flange
*   Drainage pipe
*   Explanatory Information: Drainage flanges
*   For membrane drainage connections in concrete floors: drainage flange may be either cast into the concrete slab or set into the top surface of the concrete slab or the tile bed.
*   For membrane drainage connections in other floors: drainage flange may be either set into the floor substrate or the tile bed.

## Dimensions and values
None shown

*   Explanatory Information: Drainage flanges
*   For membrane drainage connections in concrete floors: drainage flange may be either cast into the concrete slab or set into the top surface of the concrete slab or the tile bed.
*   For membrane drainage connections in other floors: drainage flange may be either set into the floor substrate or the tile bed.

## Figure
Figure 10.2.4a: Areas adjacent to baths and spas without showers for concrete, compressed fibre-cement and fibre-cement sheet flooring

## Type
Combination of a plan view and an isometric view.

## Description
The figure illustrates the required waterproofing and water resistance areas for baths and spas without showers, specifically for concrete, compressed fibre-cement, and fibre-cement sheet flooring.

Part (a) presents a plan view of a rectangular bathtub installed against a wall within a room. The floor area immediately surrounding the bathtub, including along the adjacent walls, is designated as "Waterproof" to a width of 40 mm either side of the junction. The remaining floor area within the room, outside of this specified waterproof strip, is marked as "Water resistant floor". The bathtub itself is depicted with a circular outlet or overflow symbol.

Part (b) provides an isometric, cutaway view of the same bath installation. The bathtub is shown installed on a raised structure or plinth, which is labelled "WR" (Water resistant). The floor area surrounding this plinth is indicated as "Water resistant floor" and includes a circular "Floor waste" opening. The vertical wall surfaces adjacent to the bath are designated "Water resistant" for a height of 150 mm above the "Waterproof bath/wall junction". "Waterproof junctions" are shown where the base of the bath plinth meets the floor. The joint at the top edge of the bath where it meets the finished floor is labelled "Waterproof bath lip/tile joint". On the wall above the bath, "Seal tap and bath spout penetrations" are depicted. The waterproofing requirement for these penetrations is shown as extending "Waterproof to a width of 40 mm either side of the junction" and with the waterproof junction itself extending "25 mm above finished floor level". A direct dimension of "40 mm" is also explicitly marked for the width of the waterproof area at the corner junction of the bath and wall.

## Figure
Figure 10.2.5: Bath and vessel abutting wall — areas to be protected

## Type
Section drawing, detail

## Description
The figure depicts two cross-sectional diagrams illustrating the required areas for waterproofing or water resistance where a bath or vessel abuts a wall. These areas are marked by horizontal dotted lines on the wall directly above the rim of the bath or vessel.

(a) Vessel abutting wall: This diagram shows a vessel (such as a basin or sink) in cross-section. The vessel has a curved basin, a flat rim, and a drainpipe extending downwards. Its right side is shown abutting a vertical wall. An area on the wall, extending vertically upwards from the top of the vessel's rim where it meets the wall, is marked by horizontal dotted lines. This area is labelled "WR" (Water Resistant) within the dotted region, and a leader line points to the entire dotted area as the "Waterproof vessel/wall junction". The vertical extent of this area is indicated by a dimension arrow.

(b) Wall/bath junction: This diagram shows a bath in cross-section, with its profile indicated by dashed lines for the lower part and solid lines for the rim. The bath's right side abuts a vertical wall, which is indicated by a dashed line for the lower part and a solid line for the upper part. Similar to the vessel, an area on the wall, extending vertically upwards from the top of the bath's rim where it meets the wall, is marked by horizontal dotted lines. This area is labelled "WR" within the dotted region, and a leader line points to the entire dotted area as the "Waterproof bath/wall junction". The vertical extent of this area is indicated by a dimension arrow.

The figure also includes accompanying text regarding waterproofing systems.

## Labels and annotations

## Figure
Figure 10.3.1: Measurement of heights of rooms and other spaces

## Type
Section drawing

## Description
The figure is a cross-section of a multi-level building illustrating various room and space types and their height measurement points.
The building comprises a two-storey section on the left with a gable roof, and an attached single-storey section on the right with a skillion roof.
The lower level of the left section is labelled "Non-habitable". A staircase is depicted within this room, rising from left to right.
The upper level of the left section is labelled "Habitable" and has a flat ceiling.
Above the "Habitable" room, within the gable roof space, is a section labelled "Attic". Its ceiling follows the pitch of the roof.
The single-storey section on the right is labelled "Habitable" and has a skillion roof sloping downwards from left to right. Its ceiling follows the pitch of the roof.

Vertical dimensions are shown:
- 'A' measures the full vertical height of the "Habitable" room (upper left), from its floor to its flat ceiling.
- 'C' measures the full vertical height of the "Non-habitable" room (lower left), from its floor to its flat ceiling.
- 'D' measures the vertical height from the flat ceiling of the "Habitable" room (upper left) to the underside of the pitched roof, near the right internal wall of the "Attic" space.
- 'B' measures the vertical height of the "Habitable" room (right), from its floor to the highest point of the skillion roof (left internal wall).
- 'E' is shown three times:
    - Top-left 'E': measures the vertical height from the flat ceiling of the "Habitable" room (upper left) to the underside of the pitched roof, near the left external wall of the "Attic" space.
    - Bottom-left 'E': measures the vertical clearance from the floor of the "Non-habitable" room to the underside of the staircase soffit at its lowest point (left end).
    - Right 'E': measures the vertical height from the floor of the "Habitable" room (right) to the underside of the skillion roof at its lowest point (right external wall).
- 'F' measures the vertical clearance from the floor of the "Non-habitable" room to the underside of the staircase soffit at a point further along its rise.

Horizontal dimensions are shown:
- Above the "Attic" space: a horizontal line is segmented into 'G' (from left wall), '2/3' (central portion), and 'G' (from right wall). These represent horizontal distances across the width of the "Attic".
- Below the "Non-habitable" room (lower left): a horizontal line is segmented into '2/3' (from left wall) and '1/3' (from right internal wall). These represent horizontal distances across the width of the "Non-habitable" room.
- Below the "Habitable" room (right): a horizontal line is segmented into '2/3' (from left internal wall) and '1/3' (from right external wall). These represent horizontal distances across the width of the "Habitable" room (right).

Dashed lines indicate the boundaries for measurements and the extents of the spaces.

A vertical double-line segment on the right side of an opening represents a wall jamb. A solid curved line depicts a door leaf in an open position, hinged towards the left and sweeping towards the right jamb. A dashed quarter-circle arc indicates the full extent of the door swing, starting from a point to the left of the door's pivot point on the floor line and extending to a point vertically above the right wall jamb. This area, bounded by the dashed arc, a horizontal dashed line extending left from the start of the arc, and a vertical dashed line extending upwards from the right wall jamb, is labelled "Clear space". Horizontal dimension arrows below the diagram indicate the overall width of the clear space from the left-most dashed line to the right wall jamb. Plan view

## Description
This figure is a plan view illustrating the required airborne and impact sound insulation for a common wall separating two Class 1 buildings (dwellings). The diagram shows two adjoining dwellings, labelled "DWELLING 1" on the left and "DWELLING 2" on the right, sharing a central vertical party wall.

The floor plan of DWELLING 1 from top to bottom includes a "BED" room, another "BED" room, a "BATH" room, a "LDRY" room, a "BED" room, a "KITCHEN" room, and a "LIVING" room extending across the bottom left.

The floor plan of DWELLING 2 from top to bottom includes a "GARAGE" room at the top right, a "BED" room, another "BED" room, a "LDRY" room, a "BATH" room, a "KITCHEN" room, and a "LIVING" room extending across the bottom right.

The central wall separating DWELLING 1 and DWELLING 2 is marked by an annotation "Wall separating two Class 1 buildings" pointing to it. Different segments of this common wall are shaded to indicate varying sound insulation requirements as defined in the legend.

The segment of the common wall between DWELLING 1's top "BED" room and DWELLING 2's "GARAGE" is shaded with horizontal lines.
All other segments of the common wall, specifically those between:
*   DWELLING 1's middle "BED" room and DWELLING 2's top "BED" room,

## Figure
Figure 10.7.3a: Sound insulation between buildings — Stud wall junctions

## Type
Section drawing and plan view

## Description
The figure illustrates details for achieving sound insulation at junctions between different wall types, specifically involving a stud wall. It comprises two parts:

**(a) Section**
This view shows a vertical cross-section of a building junction where a roof structure meets a wall assembly. On the left, there is a masonry wall. To its right, a timber-framed stud wall is shown with vertical studs and a horizontal top plate. The roof structure, comprising roof tiles, battens, and rafters, is pitched downwards from right to left, meeting the top of the wall assembly. A wavy, cross-hatched material is depicted filling the void between the top of the stud wall and the underside of the roof structure, and extending downwards into the cavity between the masonry wall and the stud wall. This material is shown as being packed into the space.

**(b) Plan**
This view shows a horizontal cross-section of the wall junction. On the left is the masonry wall. To its right is a cavity. Further to the right is a timber-framed stud wall, indicated by a rectangular profile with an 'X' (representing a stud) and horizontal blocking/noggings. The same wavy, cross-hatched material is shown filling the cavity between the masonry wall and the stud wall, at the junction point.

The figure illustrates the use of mineral fibre or other suitable fire resisting material to fill voids at these junctions, enhancing sound insulation.

## Labels and annotations

*   (a) Section
*   (b) Plan

## Figure
Figure 10.7.3b: Typical installation of plaster sheets for sound insulation

## Type
Section drawing, detail.

## Description
The figure depicts two different typical installations of two layers of plaster sheets on a timber stud wall frame, illustrating the staggering of joints and fixings for sound insulation. Both parts (a) and (b) show a cutaway view of a timber framed wall with vertical studs and horizontal noggings. Two layers of plaster sheets are attached to the right side of the timber frame.

**(a) Second layer positioned vertically:**
This diagram shows the second layer of plaster sheets installed with vertical joints. The first layer of plaster sheets is attached to the timber studs, with its vertical joints implied to be aligned with the studs or centrally between them. The second layer of plaster sheets is then installed over the first, such that its vertical joints are offset from both the underlying timber studs and the vertical joints of the first layer. Fixings (represented by dots) are shown securing the plaster sheets. Leader lines indicate that both the fixings and the sheet joints are staggered. The joints of the second layer are also shown taped and set.

**(b) Second layer positioned horizontally:**
This diagram shows the second layer of plaster sheets installed with horizontal joints. Similar to (a), the first layer is attached to the timber frame. The second layer is then installed over the first, with its horizontal joints clearly visible and staggered relative to the first layer (which are implied to be vertical or otherwise non-aligned with the second layer's horizontal joints). Fixings are shown as dots. No explicit dimensions or additional labels are provided for this specific configuration beyond its title.

## Labels and annotations

## Figure
Figure 10.7.5d: Single leaf of 90 mm clay brick masonry

## Type
Section drawing

## Description
The figure depicts a vertical cross-section of a single leaf of 90 mm clay brick masonry wall, showing its connection details to horizontal building elements above and below. The central element is a horizontal rectangular block representing the 90 mm clay brick masonry, shown with a speckled texture and divided into three segments by two vertical lines, suggesting mortar or control joints.

Above the masonry block, there is a gap containing a horizontal assembly. This assembly consists of a continuous wavy line spanning horizontally, flanked at both ends by square elements each containing an 'X'. *   Explanatory Information
*   The requirements of this Part are to be read in conjunction with the building sealing requirements in Part 13.4. However, it should be noted that Part 13.4 does not apply in all States and Territories.
*   12.4.3(a) requires the internal faces of masonry chimneys to be parged with a mortar to protect masonry elements and mortar beds from the corrosive by-products of combustion.
*   12.4.4 Installation of insert fireplaces and flues
*   An insert fireplace and flue must comply with the following:
*   (a) The insert fireplace and flue must be—
*   (i) tested and passed the tests required by AS/NZS 2918; and

The figure depicts acceptable installation details for a heating appliance flue system, illustrating how the flue passes through a non-masonry wall, a ceiling, and a roof structure, and the required clearances to combustible materials.

The main drawing shows a rectangular "Heating appliance" at the bottom, sitting on a base marked "See Note 2". A horizontal flue pipe extends from the right side of the heating appliance, passes through a "Non masonry wall", and continues horizontally for a short distance before turning upwards into a vertical flue pipe system. The penetration through the non-masonry wall is labelled "Detail 1". The vertical flue pipe extends upwards, passing through a horizontal "Timber framing" structure (representing a ceiling or floor) which is labelled "Detail 2", and then through an angled roof structure (also with "Timber framing") which is labelled "Detail 3". Above the roof, the flue pipe terminates. The roof structure itself is labelled "See Note 1".

Detail 1 (Wall penetration) shows a close-up of the horizontal flue pipe casing passing through a timber framed non-masonry wall. The flue pipe casing is centered horizontally within the wall opening. A "Shielding plate" is shown covering the internal face of the wall opening around the flue pipe casing. Clearances are indicated between the flue pipe casing, the shielding plate, and the wall framing.

Detail 2 (Ceiling penetration) shows a close-up of the vertical "Flue pipe" inside its "Flue pipe casing" passing upwards through a horizontal timber framed structure (e.g., a ceiling). The flue pipe casing extends above the ceiling plane. Clearances are indicated between the flue pipe, its casing, and the timber framing. ## Figure
Figure 13.3.2a: Orientation sectors

## Type
Diagram

## Description
The figure is a circular diagram representing a compass rose, divided into eight 45-degree orientation sectors. A central origin point is located at the intersection of two perpendicular black lines, representing the cardinal directions. The vertical line points upwards to True North, and downwards to South. The horizontal line points right to East, and left to West.

Eight radial lines extend from the central origin, dividing the circle into eight equal sectors. Four of these sectors are shaded grey, and four are unshaded. The shaded sectors are centered on the cardinal directions: North, East, South, and West. The unshaded sectors are centered on the inter-cardinal directions: North East, South East, South West, and North West.

Each radial line (except for the cardinal axes) is labelled with an inter-cardinal compass point and its corresponding angle in degrees, measured clockwise from True North. For example, the line defining the clockwise boundary of the North sector is labelled NNE, and the anti-clockwise boundary is labelled NNW. Curved black arrows with double arrowheads are drawn along the arc of the circle within each sector, indicating the span of the sector from one boundary line to the next.

This figure illustrates the definition of eight specific orientation sectors.

## Figure
Figure 13.3.2b: Method of measuring P and H

## Type
Section drawing

## Description
This figure is a cross-section illustrating the method for measuring P (projection) and H (height) for external shading devices in a two-storey building.

The upper part of the drawing shows the upper storey. An external shading device (e.g., an eave or hood) is positioned above a window (glazing).
*   **P (upper storey glazing)** is measured horizontally from the face of the glazing to the outermost point of the shading device.
*   **G (upper storey glazing)** is measured vertically from the top of the glazing to the underside of the shading device.
*   **H (upper storey glazing)** is measured vertically, representing the full height of the glazing.

The lower part of the drawing shows the lower storey. Another external shading device (e.g., a balcony or another projection) is positioned above a window (glazing).
*   **P (lower storey glazing)** is measured horizontally from the face of the glazing to the outermost point of the shading device.
*   **G (lower storey glazing)** is measured vertically from the top of the glazing to the underside of the shading device.
*   **H (lower storey glazing)** is measured vertically, representing the full height of the glazing.

The diagram concretely shows how P, G, and H are defined and measured in relation to the glazing and the shading device for both an upper and lower storey context. Arrows indicate the extent of each measurement.

## Figure
Figure 2: Climate zones for thermal design

## Type
Map

## Description
The figure depicts a political map of Australia, colour-coded to show eight distinct climate zones for thermal design. The map is overlaid with a grid of latitude and longitude lines. State and territory borders are outlined, and numerous cities and towns are labelled across the continent. A legend in the bottom right corner identifies the colour associated with each climate zone.

The map illustrates the following general distribution of climate zones:
- **Zone 1** (orange): Covers the northernmost tropical coastal regions, including parts of Western Australia, Northern Territory, and Queensland.
- **Zone 2** (light orange): Extends south of Zone 1, encompassing subtropical and tropical inland areas, primarily in Western Australia, Northern Territory, and Queensland.
- **Zone 3** (yellow): Predominantly covers inland northern Queensland and parts of the Northern Territory.
- **Zone 4** (pale yellow): Represents drier temperate inland regions, spanning across Western Australia, South Australia, Northern Territory, Queensland, and New South Wales.
- **Zone 5** (light green): Covers larger temperate areas, including parts of Western Australia, South Australia, Victoria, New South Wales, and Queensland.
- **Zone 6** (darker green): Concentrated in the more populated temperate coastal and near-coastal regions of South Australia, Victoria, New South Wales, and south-eastern Queensland.
- **Zone 7** (light blue): Primarily covers cooler temperate regions, including most of Tasmania and elevated areas in Victoria and New South Wales.
- **Zone 8** (dark blue): Represents alpine areas, specifically found in the high country of Tasmania, Victoria, and New South Wales.

A thin purple line indicates "Local Government Area boundary" on the map. The map also includes an ABCB logo and source information in the bottom right corner.

## Figure

## Type
Section drawing

## Description
The figure contains two cross-section diagrams illustrating site cuts and the associated zone of influence when an un-retained embankment is created. Both diagrams show a natural ground level sloping downwards from left to right, above an area of "Excavation" and a "Zone of influence".

The top diagram depicts a site cut commencing at an "Allotment boundary", marked by a vertical dashed line on the left. The "Natural ground level" starts at the allotment boundary and slopes downwards to the right. Below this, a triangular region labelled "Excavation" is shown, extending from the natural ground level. Adjacent to the excavation and towards the allotment boundary, a shaded trapezoidal area is labelled "Zone of influence". A vertical dimension 'H' is shown from the natural ground level at the allotment boundary downwards to the bottom edge of the Zone of influence. A horizontal dimension 'L' extends from the allotment boundary to the right, to the lowest extent of the site cut. The rightmost vertical extent of the cut is labelled "Site cut". A sloped line, referred to as line A-A in the notes, forms the boundary between the excavation and the zone of influence, and also the bottom boundary of both. A solid black square with the letter 'A' inside is located at the intersection of the natural ground level and the allotment boundary on the left, and another 'A' is at the bottom right of the "Site cut" line.

The bottom diagram is similar, but shows a simplified outline of a house structure situated on the "Natural ground level" at the allotment boundary. In this case, the vertical dimension 'H' is measured from the bottom of the house's footing downwards to the bottom edge of the Zone of influence. The 'A' marking is at the bottom left corner of the house's footing. The horizontal dimension 'L', "Zone of influence", "Excavation", and "Site cut" elements are arranged identically to the top diagram.

The figure illustrates the extent of excavation and the resulting zone of influence in relation to a site boundary or an adjacent structure, highlighting the H:L ratio that defines the maximum embankment slope.

## Figure
Figure 4.2.11a: Splice, L and T intersections

## Type
Detail drawings (plan view)

## Description
The figure depicts three different arrangements for reinforcing mesh or bars: a splice, a "T" intersection, and an "L" intersection corner.

**(a) Splice:** This sub-diagram shows a top-down view of two rectangular sections of reinforcing mesh overlapping. The upper mesh section overlaps the lower mesh section. Both mesh sections consist of parallel lines with four circular dots representing transverse wires. The text indicates that the two outermost wires of the top mesh section are lapping over the two outermost wires of the bottom mesh section.

**(b) "T" intersection:** This sub-diagram shows a top-down view of a "T" shaped intersection formed by two sections of reinforcing mesh or bars. A horizontal mesh section runs left to right, and a vertical mesh section intersects it perpendicularly at its midpoint, extending both above and below the horizontal section. The text indicates that the mesh should lap full width at this intersection.

**(c) "L" intersection corner:** This sub-diagram shows a top-down view of a 90-degree "L" shaped corner formed by reinforcing bars or mesh. Two parallel lines represent the outer bar, which curves around the corner. An inner bar is also shown, but it does not extend as far around the bend. A vertical dimension line with arrows indicates the required continuance length for the outer bar after the bend.

The overall depth of this element is also marked 'D', with a thickened portion extending at least 200 mm below the underside of the main slab. ## Type
Section drawing

## Description
The figure depicts a cross-section of a reinforced concrete slab with a central rectangular recess. The overall slab has a nominal depth, D, shown at the left and right edges. The top surface of the slab is flat at the nominal depth, then steps down to form a recess. The depth of this recess, d, is measured vertically from the nominal top surface of the slab to the top surface of the recessed area. Below the recessed area, the bottom surface of the slab is horizontal, maintaining a constant thickness below the recess. On either side of the recessed area, the slab thickness increases from the recess depth to the nominal slab depth. This thickening is achieved by the bottom surface of the slab sloping downwards and outwards from beneath the recess, eventually meeting the nominal bottom surface of the full-depth slab. The horizontal extent of this thickened section on each side of the recess is labelled L. Reinforcement bars, represented by solid black circles, are embedded within the lower portion of the concrete slab. The reinforcement follows the profile of the slab, running horizontally in the full-depth sections, curving upwards through the thickened sections, and running horizontally again within the reduced depth section under the recess. The diagram illustrates the specified dimensions and configuration for slab recesses.

## Figure
Figure 4.2.5: Foundations for footings and slabs

## Type
Section drawing

## Description
The figure depicts three options (a), (b), and (c) for foundations on cut and filled sites, illustrating different methods for preparing the ground beneath footings and slabs. Each option is a cross-sectional view of a foundation system on sloping ground.

**Option (a) Option 1** shows a concrete slab or footing system at the top. Beneath the slab is a layer of "Controlled fill". To the right of the slab, the natural ground slopes downwards, with an annotation indicating "Strip topsoil before filling" below the location where fill would be placed. To the left of the slab, a sloped embankment is formed by "Compacted fill", which has a specified "Slope ratio not greater than 1 : 2". A layer of "Reuse stripped topsoil (suggested)" covers the sloped compacted fill. The entire filled area under the slab and extending to the right and below the compacted fill is designated as "Rolled or controlled fill", indicated with horizontal dashed lines. A horizontal dimension line above the controlled fill layer beneath the slab indicates a minimum width before the sloping embankment begins.

**Option (b) Option 2** shows a concrete slab with a "Deepened edge beam or bulk piers" at the top. This edge beam extends downwards into a layer of "Additional rolled or controlled fill if bulk piers used". This layer is situated above "Compacted fill", which forms a sloped embankment to the left. The sloped compacted fill has a "Slope ratio not greater than 1 : 2". The fill material beneath the deepened edge beam and the compacted fill is indicated as "Rolled or controlled fill". A horizontal dimension line indicates a minimum width for the area directly beneath the edge beam before the sloping embankment.

**Option (c) Option 3** shows a concrete slab system supported by a "Deepened edge beam or retaining wall" at the top left. The deepened edge beam or retaining wall extends vertically downwards, appearing to penetrate into undisturbed ground. The concrete slab to the right of the wall rests on a layer of "Rolled or controlled fill", which extends horizontally from the wall and then slopes downwards to the right, following the contour of the natural ground.

## Figure
Figure 4.2.8: Acceptable vapour barrier and damp-proofing membrane location

## Type
Section drawing

## Description
This figure presents three detailed section drawings, labelled (a), (b), and (c), illustrating acceptable configurations for vapour barriers and damp-proofing membranes at the edge of a slab-on-ground foundation, specifically where it meets a masonry wall. The figures demonstrate how these membranes are integrated with different edge rebate designs and ground levels to provide damp-proofing.

Drawing (a), titled "Minimum rebate for cavity masonry or veneer wall", shows a concrete slab-on-ground with a cavity masonry wall constructed above it. A vapour barrier or damp-proofing membrane extends horizontally beneath the slab, turns upwards at the outer edge, and passes through a rebate in the slab edge. It then extends vertically within the wall cavity, terminating above the finished ground level. The finished ground, including paving, slopes downwards away from the wall. The membrane's termination point is indicated at or just above the finished ground level.

Drawing (b), titled "Deep edge rebate alternative", depicts a concrete slab-on-ground with a masonry wall. A vapour barrier and damp-proofing membrane extends horizontally beneath the slab, turns sharply downwards into a deep, stepped rebate at the slab edge, then turns sharply upwards into the wall cavity, terminating above the finished ground level. The finished ground, including paving, slopes downwards away from the wall. A vertical dimension is indicated from the finished ground level to the lowest point of the downward turn of the membrane within the rebate.

Drawing (c), titled "Masonry alternative", shows a concrete slab-on-ground supported by a masonry foundation wall, which rests on a separate footing. A vapour barrier extends horizontally beneath the slab, turns upwards into a rebate at the slab edge, and terminates within the masonry wall above the slab level. The finished ground, including paving, slopes downwards away from the wall, and is shown below the slab level.

## Figure
Figure 5.7.6: Typical window installation for unreinforced single skin masonry

## Type
Section drawing

## Description
The figure presents five detailed section drawings illustrating typical window installation methods for unreinforced single skin masonry, focusing on head, jamb, and various sill fixing details.

Sub-figure (a) "Head fixing" shows a section of the top of a window frame installed beneath a concrete filled lintel within a masonry wall. A masonry anchor secures the window frame to the lintel. Sealant is applied between the window frame and the surrounding masonry, and an external coating is visible on the masonry surface, specified to be applied before window fitting.

Sub-figure (b) "Jamb fixing" depicts a vertical section through the side (jamb) of a window frame. The frame is anchored into the masonry wall, which is topped by a concrete filled lintel. Sealant is applied between the window frame and the masonry. An external coating is shown on the masonry, to be applied before the window is fitted.

Sub-figure (c) "Sill fixing - 1" illustrates an external sill detail where a sill tile is adhered to the masonry below the window frame using exterior tile adhesive. The figure depicts a map of Australia divided into three climatic zones (ZONE A, ZONE B, and ZONE C) based on relative humidity. The zones are delineated by irregular lines.

The figure illustrates two typical connection details for a universal steel beam to a steel column.

The steel column is depicted as a hollow rectangular section. An adjacent smaller diagram shows an elevation view of this connection, depicting the two steel beams as I-sections sitting side-by-side on top of the steel column.

Plan view

## Description
The figure is a plan view depicting two adjacent room layouts, distinguishing between what is considered a "Sanitary compartment" and "NOT a sanitary compartment".

On the left, there is a room entered via a door that swings inwards from the top. Inside this room, a toilet fixture is positioned centrally at the bottom. This room is labelled "Sanitary compartment".

To the right, there is a larger, L-shaped room, also entered via a door that swings inwards from its top-left corner. This larger room is labelled "NOT a sanitary compartment".

*   **Sarking-type material**: A material such as a *reflective insulation* or other flexible membrane of a type normally used for a purpose such as waterproofing, vapour management or thermal reflectance.

## Figure
Figure 7.3.2b: Fixing of tile requirements — Minimum tile fixing requirements - Wind class N1/N2

## Type
Plan view

## Description
The figure illustrates two plan views, "Option 1" and "Option 2", for minimum tile fixing requirements on a roof for wind classes N1/N2. Each option shows a rectangular section of a tiled roof, viewed from above, with individual tiles laid in courses. Shaded tiles represent fixed tiles, while unshaded tiles represent unfixed tiles. The top boundary is labelled "Ridge line", the bottom boundary is "Eave line or outside edge of roof", and the left and right vertical boundaries are "Edge of roof".

**Option 1:**
In the main body of the roof (the "field of roof"), tiles are fixed in alternating courses. The top visible course has all tiles fixed (shaded), the course below it has no tiles fixed (unshaded), and this pattern repeats downwards. There are five courses shown in the field of roof, with the 1st, 3rd, and 5th courses (from the top down) having all tiles fixed, and the 2nd and 4th courses having no tiles fixed. Along the bottom edge of the roof, specifically in the second course up from the "Eave line or outside edge of roof", all tiles are fixed (shaded).

**Option 2:**
In the main body of the roof (the "field of roof"), tiles are fixed in every second position within every course. For each course, alternating tiles are fixed (shaded) and unfixed (unshaded). The pattern is staggered between adjacent courses such that a fixed tile in one course is positioned above an unfixed tile in the course below it, and vice versa. For example, the top course starts with an unfixed tile on the left, followed by a fixed tile, then unfixed, and so on. The course below it starts with a fixed tile, followed by an unfixed tile, and so on. This alternating pattern of fixed and unfixed tiles within each course is consistent across all courses shown in the field of roof. Along the bottom edge of the roof, similar to Option 1, all tiles in the second course up from the "Eave line or outside edge of roof" are fixed (shaded).

This figure is a cross-section drawing illustrating the construction of a bedded and pointed valley for a tiled roof in high rainfall areas. The drawing shows the structural and finishing elements of a roof valley where two roof planes meet.

## Figure
Figure 7.3.5: Typical installation of anti-ponding device/board

## Type
Section drawing

## Description
This figure is a cross-section drawing illustrating the typical installation of an anti-ponding device and sarking at a tiled roof eave with an attached gutter.

The drawing depicts a roof assembly sloping downwards from right to left. From top to bottom, the visible layers include:
1.  **Roof tiles**: These are the outermost layer, extending beyond the fascia and gutter at the eave. A dimension line indicates the horizontal extent of the tile overhang beyond the vertical plane of the fascia/gutter.
2.  **Sarking**: Shown beneath the tiles, continuous and following the slope of the roof.
3.  **Anti-ponding device**: Positioned directly beneath the sarking and above the roof rafters. It appears as a continuous board following the roof slope.
4.  **Battens**: A single roof batten is shown supporting the tiles. It is placed on top of the anti-ponding device, which in turn rests on the rafters.
5.  **Rafters**: Sloping structural timbers forming the roof frame.
6.  **Fascia**: A vertical board attached to the end of the rafters at the eave.
7.  **Eaves gutter**: Attached to the fascia board.

An arrow points from the anti-ponding device towards the gutter, indicating the path for water flow. Another arrow points to the sarking. A dimension line shows a vertical clearance measurement below the first batten. The drawing shows how the sarking and anti-ponding device work together to manage water at the eave, with the tile overhang ensuring water discharges into the gutter.

## Labels and annotations

## Description
The figure depicts four separate cross-sectional detail drawings illustrating different methods for fixing timber wall cladding.

1.  **Shiplap weather board:** This drawing shows a vertical cross-section of two overlapping shiplap weatherboards fixed to a wall frame. The top board's lower, rebated edge sits over the upper, rebated edge of the board below. Nails are driven diagonally downwards through the upper portion of the top board's rebate, into the wall frame. Measurements indicate the nail's position relative to the rebate and the lower edge of the board. The general timber cladding is labelled.
2.  **Splayed weather board:** This drawing shows a vertical cross-section of two overlapping splayed weatherboards fixed to a wall frame. The top board's lower, splayed edge overlaps the top, splayed edge of the board below it. A packing piece is shown filling the void behind the overlapping section, between the cladding and the wall frame. Nails are driven diagonally downwards through the top board, piercing both boards, into the wall frame. Measurements indicate the nail's position relative to the upper edge of the board and the extent of the overlap. Text specifies the need for full length packing.
3.  **Section at lower part of weatherboard building:** This drawing shows a vertical cross-section of the lower part of a wall clad with splayed weatherboards. The lowest splayed weatherboard is shown fixed to the wall frame, with its lower edge resting on a plinth. A packing piece is shown behind the plinth, filling the space between the plinth and the wall frame. Below the plinth, and flush with its outer face, is stump lining. The weatherboards are shown fixed with nails.
4.  **Shiplap weather board fixed through batten:** This drawing shows a vertical cross-section of two overlapping shiplap weatherboards fixed through vertical timber battens to a wall frame. The vertical timber battens are shown attached to the wall frame. The shiplap weatherboards are fixed to these battens using nails driven horizontally through the thicker part of the cladding, through the batten, and into the wall frame. ## Type
Section drawing

## Description
The figure is a section drawing illustrating the relationship between a roof eave projection and the vertical position of an opening in an external wall for weather protection.
The drawing shows the upper portion of an external wall in section, with internal framing (indicated by crosses) and external cladding. Above the wall, a roof eave structure extends outwards horizontally, with a gutter at its outer edge. The roof structure itself slopes upwards from left to right.
A dashed line indicates the bottom edge of the roof eave structure where it meets the external wall.
A dimension line labelled 'A' indicates the horizontal projection of the eave, measured from the outer face of the external wall cladding to a vertical line dropped from the outermost edge of the eave (just above the gutter).
A dimension line labelled 'B' indicates the vertical distance from the dashed line representing the bottom of the eave structure to the top of an implied opening in the wall below.
A leader line connects an annotation to the implied top of the opening in the wall, indicating the location where flashing would typically be applied. The figure illustrates a condition under which flashing to the top of an opening may be omitted based on the relationship between dimensions A and B.

*   A
*   B

*   Section

    7.5.6(a)(i) applies ‘where practicable’ because it is often impractical to extend the flashing 110 mm beyond the reveal; for example, where openings are positioned adjacent to a corner or where two windows are within 110 mm of each other. The figure presents an elevation view of three adjacent Class 1 buildings, illustrating the concept of separating walls. Each building has a pitched gable roof. The left and middle buildings are separated by a vertical wall (hatched) that extends from the ground line up to the intersection point (valley) of their respective roofs. The middle and right buildings are separated by another vertical wall (hatched) that extends from the ground line, penetrates through both roofs, and rises above them, forming a parapet. The image concretely depicts two configurations for separating walls between Class 1 buildings: one terminating at the roof line and one extending above it.

*   Separating walls
*   Class 1 building
*   Class 1 building
*   Class 1 building
*   Elevation

None shown

## Notes
*   **Figure Notes**
*   In Volume Two a separating wall may also be known as a party wall and typically is *required* to be *fire-resisting* construction (see ABCB Housing Provisions Parts 9.2 and 9.3).
*   **Service:** For the purposes of Section J in Volume One, means a mechanical or electrical system that uses energy to provide *air-conditioning*, mechanical ventilation, heated water supply, artificial lighting, vertical transport and the like within a building, but which does not include—
    *   (a) systems used solely for emergency purposes; and
    *   (b) cooking facilities; and
    *   (c) portable appliances.
*   **Service station:** A garage which is not a *private garage* and is for the servicing of vehicles, other than only washing, cleaning or polishing.
*   **Shaft:** The walls and other parts of a building bounding—
    *   (a) a well, other than an *atrium well*; or
    *   (b) a vertical chute, duct or similar passage, but not a chimney or flue.
*   *VIC Shared accommodation building*
*   **Shower area:** The area affected by water from a shower, including a shower over a bath and for a shower area that is—
    *   (a) Enclosed — the area enclosed by walls or screens including hinged or sliding doors that contain the spread of water to within that space; or
    *   (b) Unenclosed — the area where, under normal use, water from the shower rose is not contained within the shower area.
*   **Shower screen:** The panels, doors or windows enclosing or partially enclosing a *shower area*.
*   **Single leaf masonry:** Outer walls constructed with a single thickness of masonry unit.
*   **Site:** The part of the allotment of land on which a building stands or is to be erected.
*   **Sitework:** Work on or around a *site*, including earthworks, preparatory to or associated with the construction, *alteration*, demolition or removal of a building.
*   *NSW Small live music or arts venue*
*   *SA Small arts venue*
*   **Small-scale Technology Certificate:** A certificate issued under the Commonwealth Government’s Small-scale Renewable Energy Scheme.
*   **Smoke-and-heat vent:** A vent, located in or near the roof for smoke and hot gases to escape if there is a fire in the building.
*   *NSW Smoke-Developed Index*
*   **Smoke-Developed Index:** The index number for smoke as determined by an *Accredited Testing Laboratory* in accordance with AS/NZS 1530.3.

## Figure
Figure 9.2.3a: Typical construction of external walls

## Type
Section drawings

## Description
This figure presents four different section drawings illustrating typical construction details for external walls at the roofline, demonstrating the integration of non-combustible materials for roofing, flashing, gutters, fascia, and eaves lining.

**(a) Gable construction**
This drawing shows a vertical section through a gable end. An external wall, depicted as a masonry or solid structure, extends vertically upwards to support the roof structure. Above the top of the wall, a roofing batten is positioned horizontally. Non-combustible roofing and flashing are shown covering the batten and extending over the top of the external wall. The flashing forms a cap over the wall.

**(b) Gutter on face of wall**
This drawing illustrates an eaves detail with a gutter attached to the face of the external wall. The external wall is a cavity wall, with an outer leaf of brickwork and an inner framed structure. The roof structure slopes upwards from the external wall, with non-combustible roofing placed on top. A non-combustible fascia and gutter assembly is attached to the external face of the outer brickwork leaf, positioned below the edge of the non-combustible roofing. The brickwork of the outer leaf is shown cut around a truss or rafter, which forms part of the roof structure.

**(c) Gutter on top of wall**
This drawing shows an eaves detail where the gutter is placed on top of the external wall. The external wall is a cavity wall, similar to (b), with an outer leaf of masonry and an inner framed structure. The roof structure slopes upwards from the external wall, covered by non-combustible roofing. A non-combustible gutter and flashing assembly is seated directly on top of the outer masonry leaf of the external wall. The flashing from this assembly extends upwards, beneath the non-combustible roofing.

**(d) Eaves construction**

## Type
Section drawing and plan view.

## Description
The figure illustrates the criteria for identifying an open carport, presenting two examples.

**(a) Example A**
This is a section drawing showing a Class 1 building adjacent to a carport. The carport has a roof that extends from the Class 1 building. There is an "Allotment boundary" line to the right of the carport. A shaded area is indicated between the Class 5 building and the carport, and between the carport and the allotment boundary. The roof covering of the carport is shown to be set back from the Class 1 building and the allotment boundary. Compliance notes specify material requirements for roof covering and ceiling lining, and conditions for timber posts, beams, and wall cladding adjacent to a boundary. It defines when a side of a carport is considered open based on the absence of roof covering over a specified shaded area.

**(b) Example B**
This is a plan view showing a rectangular Class 1 building connected to a rectangular carport. The carport has dimensions of 3 m (width) and 6 m (length). One 6 m side of the carport is adjacent to an "Allotment boundary". Two sides of the carport, one 3 m side and one 6 m side, are labelled "Open". The 6 m side adjacent to the allotment boundary is described as "Side of carport less than 500 mm from allotment boundary, therefore side is considered closed". A "Carport calculation" box demonstrates how to calculate the "Open side / Perimeter" ratio for this specific carport, arriving at a value of 1/3, and states that this satisfies the exemption criteria.

## Description
The figure illustrates the requirements for non-combustible infill panels in a carport, particularly at the interface between a dwelling and an attached carport.

Part (a) is an elevation view showing a dwelling on the left connected to a carport on the right. Both structures have pitched roofs. The carport's roof slopes down from the dwelling's roof. The roof cladding over the carport is identified as "Non-combustible roof cladding". A vertical dashed line to the right of the carport is labelled "Boundary line". A specific section of the wall where the dwelling meets the carport, near the roofline, is highlighted with an oval and a callout indicating "Detail (see below)".

Part (b) is a detail section, labelled "Detail – option 1", showing a vertical cross-section through the highlighted wall area. Above the wall structure, the roof is depicted. The wall contains a cavity with structural studs (represented by 'X' symbols). This cavity is filled with "Infill of non-combustible material". To the left of the wall, a ceiling, labelled "Ceiling to dwelling", extends to meet the wall structure. The space to the right of the wall is identified as the "Carport".

Part (c) is another detail section, labelled "Detail – option 2", also showing a vertical cross-section through the wall. Similar to option 1, the roof is above the wall structure, and a "Ceiling to dwelling" meets the wall from the left. However, instead of infill material within the wall cavity, the internal face of the wall structure, facing the carport, is covered with a "Non-combustible lining". The space to the right of the wall is identified as the "Carport".

The figure illustrates two methods for ensuring non-combustible construction in the infill panels of a carport where it adjoins a dwelling.

Section drawing

This figure is a vertical cross-section drawing illustrating the construction of a hollow separating wall system to accommodate services within a cavity. The drawing shows two parallel, hollow separating walls, each depicted with diagonal hatching. Between these two walls, a cavity is present. Within the cavity, towards the top of the depicted section, a horizontal piece of framing is installed, spanning the width of the cavity and seemingly supported by the inner faces of both hollow walls. On the right-hand hollow separating wall, an electrical outlet is shown embedded in the wall, with an electrical cable extending from its rear into the cavity, connecting to the area of the framing. ## Figure

## Type
Section detail

## Description
A vertical cross-section showing the construction detail of a preformed shower base where it joins the wall and floor:

- **Floor substrate:** Sits horizontally at the base of the assembly.
- **Shower base support:** A cross-hatched support layer positioned directly over the floor substrate under the base of the preformed shower base.
- **Preformed shower base:** Rests on the shower base support. The profile slopes downwards to the left towards the shower side, while its outer perimeter forms an upturned vertical lip that sits recessed into the wall.
- **Wall rebate:** A recess cut or framed into the wall structure ("Wall rebate to accomodate shower base") that accepts the upturned outer rim of the shower base.
- **Water-resistant surface material of the wall:** A vertical wall lining layer (indicated by diagonal cross-hatching) suspended vertically above a horizontal step on the rim of the shower base, positioned outward of the shower base's vertical upstand.
- **Waterproof sealant:** A solid-filled bead positioned directly under the bottom edge of the water-resistant surface material, sealing the gap between the wall lining and the horizontal step/shoulder of the preformed shower base.
- **Shower side:** The interior area to the left of the preformed shower base.

## Figure
Figure 10.5.1: Method of determining areas of openings for borrowed light

## Type
Isometric diagram

## Description
The figure consists of two isometric line diagrams illustrating the method for calculating the required minimum areas of openings when natural light is borrowed from an adjoining room. Both diagrams show two adjoining rectangular rooms, "Room A" and "Room B", sharing an internal dividing wall. 

In both diagrams:
- **Room A** is an outer room with an external wall containing an external window opening labelled **A**.
- **Room B** is an inner room situated directly behind Room A, separated by an internal partition wall shown with a dashed line at the floor.
- Dimension **a** is the width of Room A (and Room B).
- Dimension **b** is the total combined depth of both Room A and Room B, measured from the external front wall of Room A to the rear wall of Room B.
- Dimension **c** is the depth of Room B, measured from the internal dividing wall to the rear wall of Room B.

The two diagrams depict different types of internal openings between Room A and Room B:
- **Top diagram:** Shows opening **B** configured as an internal doorway opening with an open door leaf in the dividing wall between Room A and Room B.
- **Bottom diagram:** Shows opening **B** configured as an internal window opening located centrally in the dividing wall between Room A and Room B.

To the right of each diagram are the formulas for calculating opening areas:
- Area of external opening $A = \frac{a \times b}{10}\text{ m}^2$ (10% of the total combined floor area of Room A and Room B).
- Area of internal opening $B = \frac{a \times c}{10}\text{ m}^2$ (10% of the floor area of Room B).

## Labels and annotations
- Figure 10.5.1: Method of determining areas of openings for borrowed light
- A (external opening on the front wall of Room A, shown in both diagrams)
- B (internal opening between Room A and Room B, shown in both diagrams)
- Room A (shown in both diagrams)
- Room B (shown in both diagrams)
- a (dimension indicator for room width, shown in both diagrams)
- b (dimension indicator for total combined room depth, shown in both diagrams)
- c (dimension indicator for depth of Room B, shown in both diagrams)
- $\mathrm{A = \frac{a \times b}{10} \ m^2}$ (shown to the right of each diagram)
- $\mathrm{B = \frac{a \times c}{10} \ m^2}$ (shown to the right of each diagram)
- Explanatory Information: Explanatory Figure 10.5.1
- A *roof light* generally receives greater exposure to sunlight than a *window* because of its orientation to the sky and consequently, the size of a *roof light* as a percentage of the *floor area* served is permitted to be smaller than for a

## Dimensions and values

- $\mathrm{B = \frac{a \times c}{10} \ m^2}$ (minimum area of internal borrowed light opening B)
